segments.text: Accountability ensures that those who exercise public power must explain their decisions, face genuine scrutiny, and — where rules are breached or performance fails — be subject to correction or sanction. This unit substantially deepens the accountability material already introduced in the Public Administration chapter’s Unit XI, adding a specific focus on the symbolic-versus-substantive distinction, comparative perspectives, and a fuller taxonomy of accountability types.

exists when institutions or procedures create only an appearance of control without producing meaningful information flow, genuine questioning, actual correction, or real consequences — a body that exists on paper, holds occasional meetings, but never actually alters a decision or sanctions a wrongdoer, is symbolically but not substantively accountable. Distinguishing symbolic compliance from substantive answerability and enforcement is precisely the analytical skill this topic rewards.

Comparative governance analysis (comparing accountability arrangements across countries or regions) helps identify genuine institutional design differences and alternatives, but the syllabus’s important caution is to
avoid uncritically copying one country’s model

without carefully considering the differing legal, political, and administrative context it originated in — an accountability mechanism that works well in one constitutional and political setting may fail or even backfire in a different context. When comparing two specific accountability arrangements, the recommended comparison dimensions are purpose, structure, authority, process, strengths, limitations, and the context in which each design actually works better. When drawing on contemporary studies, always note the methodology behind any perception survey or composite indicator relied upon (echoing the same caution already made about the WGI indicators in Unit III).

operates through courts and legal mechanisms testing whether public authorities acted within law, respected legally protected rights, and followed required procedure — directly paralleling judicial control as covered in the Public Administration chapter’s Unit XI.

operates within the executive branch through hierarchy, internal controls, audit, inspection, disciplinary systems, and performance management — a form of accountability that does not require external actors at all, since it is built into the executive’s own internal structure.

every technical judgment made (a doctor’s specific clinical decision, an engineer’s specific technical calculation) — professional accountability substitutes peer and professional-body judgment for direct hierarchical observation in these cases.

: private organizations are primarily accountable to owners, customers, regulators, and contract/commercial law; public bodies face all of these plus additional democratic, constitutional, budgetary, and public-interest accountability that a private organization simply does not face in the same form — the added layer, not present in the private sector, is the exam-relevant point here.
